story:
The oldest shape highlighted a person's head. Its meaning moved from that high point to the sky above.

From a head held high to the sky overhead: that is the meaning in 天空 (tiān kōng), “sky.”
hint: Use 天空 to describe the sky above.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 天: sky

story:
The earth component 土 gives the meaning, while 也 gives a sound clue.

The 土 part keeps the meaning grounded in 土地 (tǔ dì), “land”; 也 helps with the sound.
hint: Use 土地 to talk about land or ground.
visual: Three layers of ground with two little shoots above.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 地: ground

story:
Early writing showed a small mound rising from the ground, sometimes with dots for grains of earth.

The mound of earth leads directly to 泥土 (ní tǔ), the everyday word for soil.
hint: Use 泥土 to describe soil or dirt.
visual: A mound of earth holds the roots of a growing plant.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 土: soil

story:
An early shape resembled a stone chime, an instrument made of rock. That image came to mean stone itself.

The old stone instrument explains why 石头 (shí tou) now means an ordinary stone.
hint: Use 石头 to refer to a stone.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 石: stone

story:
Early forms put tiny grains beside water.

Grains by water make a useful clue to 沙子 (shā zi), sand along a shore.
hint: Use 沙子 to describe the physical material of sand.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 沙: sand

story:
云 is the simplified form used for “cloud”; the traditional form is 雲.

In 白云 (bái yún), the first character gives the color and 云 gives the cloud: “white cloud.”
hint: 白云 is the standard way to say white cloud.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 云: cloud

story:
In early writing, drops fell beneath a line for sky or cloud. The weather was visible in the shape.

The falling marks in the old shape match 下雨 (xià yǔ), “to rain.”
hint: 下雨 is the common verb phrase for raining.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 雨: rain

story:
An old form combined rain with small marks like falling flakes; another part helped with the sound.

Rain and tiny flakes in the old form point to 下雪 (xià xuě), “to snow.”
hint: Use 下雪 to talk about the weather snowing.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 雪: snow

story:
The older 風 used 凡 as a sound clue. The simplified 风 has fewer strokes.

Use 大风 (dà fēng) for strong wind; its meaning is the movement of air.
hint: Use with adjectives like big to describe strong wind.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 风: wind

story:
One early form paired a lightning mark with wheel-like shapes, comparing thunder to a rumbling cart.

The old comparison with a rumbling wheel helps recall 打雷 (dǎ léi), “to thunder.”
hint: Describes the sound of a storm.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 雷: thunder

story:
An early lightning shape was later paired with rain. The modern 电 grew from that idea of a flash in a storm.

Lightning in the older form became 电, used in 电灯 (diàn dēng) for an electric light.
hint: Used for power and light devices.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 电: electricity

story:
The older 氣 once also referred to grain given as a gift. Later it came to name air and breath.

Its air-and-breath use lives in 空气 (kōng qì), the everyday word for air.
hint: Refers to the atmosphere or breath.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 气: air

story:
Early writing put block-like marks beside water to show it had frozen into ice.

Water turning solid is the link to 冰水 (bīng shuǐ), “ice water.”
hint: Use this word when ordering cold drinks or describing frozen water.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 冰: ice

story:
The water part carries the meaning of river; an older second part supplied its sound.

Water in the character connects 小河 (xiǎo hé) with a small river.
hint: Refers to a natural flowing body of water like a stream.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 河: river

story:
The water part points to the sea, while 每 supplied a sound clue in the older form.

The water sign leads to 大海 (dà hǎi), the wide sea.
hint: Describes the vast ocean or large saltwater bodies.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 海: sea

story:
江 pairs water with 工 as a sound clue. It first named the Yangtze before it came to mean large rivers more broadly.

Its early link to the Yangtze survives in the name 长江 (Cháng Jiāng).
hint: Used for major, long rivers like the Yangtze.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 江: large river

story:
The three water strokes tell you this is about water; 胡 supplies the sound in 湖.

The water strokes also belong in 湖水 (hú shuǐ), “lake water.”
hint: Use this word when describing large bodies of water in nature.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 湖: lake

story:
泉 means a natural spring, where water comes out of the ground.

泉水 (quán shuǐ) names water from a natural spring.
hint: Refers to water coming directly from a natural underground source.
visual: Fresh water flowing from a spring
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 泉: spring

story:
The water strokes on the left of 波 mark a water-related word.

The water clue matches 波浪 (bō làng), the word for waves.
hint: Commonly used to describe the rhythmic movement of water surfaces.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 波: wave

story:
The water strokes on the left of 浪 mark a water-related word.

海浪 (hǎi làng) names sea waves; the water strokes point to their setting.
hint: Used for large, forceful waves typically found in the ocean.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 浪: large wave

story:
The plant component 艹 in 花 points to a flower.

The plant top matches 花园 (huā yuán), a garden full of flowers.
hint: Use 花园 to describe a place full of flowers.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 花: flower

story:
The plant component 艹 in 草 points to grass.

The plant top also appears in 小草 (xiǎo cǎo), the word for little grass.
hint: 小草 refers to small blades of grass.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 草: grass

story:
竹 means bamboo; its written form has two matching halves.

竹子 (zhú zi) is the everyday word for the bamboo plant.
hint: 竹子 is the standard word for bamboo.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 竹: bamboo

story:
叶 is the simplified form of 葉 and means leaf.

树叶 (shù yè) is a tree leaf; 树 names the tree and 叶 names its leaf.
hint: 树叶 is the common term for tree leaves.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 叶: leaf

story:
木, the tree component, appears in 树.

大树 (dà shù) combines 大, big, with 树, tree: a big tree.
hint: 大树 means a big, tall tree.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 树: tree

story:
木, the tree component, appears in 根, root.

树根 (shù gēn) is a tree root, the part below the trunk.
hint: 树根 refers to the roots of a tree.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 根: root

story:
木 marks a tree-related meaning, while 支 supplies the sound.

The wood clue points to 树枝 (shù zhī), a branch of a tree.
hint: 树枝 is the word for a tree branch.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 枝: branch

story:
Three copies of 木 stand for many trees. That is the old construction behind 森, a forest.

Three trees become many; 森林 (sēn lín) is the common word for forest.
hint: 森林 describes a large, dense forest area.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 森: dense forest

story:
Early writing scattered star marks across the sky; 生 supplied a sound clue in the developed character.

The old cluster of stars leads to 星星 (xīng xing), “star.”
hint: 星星 is the word for stars in the sky.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 星: star

story:
An early form placed fire above a kneeling person, conveying light shining down.

Light shining from the early fire shape connects to 阳光 (yáng guāng), sunlight.
hint: 阳光 refers to the light from the sun.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 光: light

story:
A roof-like cave shape marks a hollow place; 工 helps with sound. The meaning later widened to empty space.

The old hollow-place meaning leads toward open space; 天空 (tiān kōng) means sky.
hint: Used in 天空 to describe the open sky.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 空: empty; sky

story:
An early form brought a plant and the sun together, with another part helping the sound: new growth in spring.

Sun and new plant growth belong to 春天 (chūn tiān), springtime.
hint: Used in 春天 to name the spring season.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 春: spring season

story:
Early forms show a person looking up beneath the hot sun. The modern strokes no longer show that scene clearly.

The person beneath the hot sun points to 夏天 (xià tiān), the summer season.
hint: Used in 夏天 to name the summer season.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 夏: summer

story:
One early interpretation sees a chirping cricket; later writing uses grain, fitting the harvest season.

Cricket calls and ripe grain both belong to 秋天 (qiū tiān), autumn.
hint: Used in 秋天 to name the autumn season.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 秋: autumn

story:
Early 冬 looked like a cord knotted at both ends: an ending. The season came to name the end of the year.

The old idea of an ending fits 冬天 (dōng tiān), the last, cold season of the year.
hint: Used in 冬天 to name the winter season.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 冬: winter

story:
The ice component gives a cold clue, while 令 supplies the sound.

The ice clue helps with 冷水 (lěng shuǐ), cold water.
hint: Used in 冷水 to describe cold water.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 冷: cold

story:
The older 熱 included fire below; another part supplied the sound.

Fire marks the heat in 热水 (rè shuǐ), hot water.
hint: Used in 热水 to describe hot water.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 热: hot

story:
日, the sun component, appears in 晴, a word for clear weather.

The sun component makes sense in 晴天 (qíng tiān), a clear sunny day.
hint: Used in 晴天 to describe a sunny day.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 晴: clear weather

story:
The older 陰 named the side of a hill away from sunlight. That shaded idea also suits an overcast day.

The shaded side of a hill helps recall 阴天 (yīn tiān), an overcast day.
hint: Used in 阴天 to describe a cloudy day.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 阴: overcast; shade

story:
The older 陽 pictured sunlight reaching a hillside, the sunny side of the place.

The sunlit side of a hill leads to 太阳 (tài yáng), the sun.
hint: Used in 太阳 to name the sun.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 阳: sunny side

story:
The older 霧 has rain above and a sound clue below.

The rain component belongs with 大雾 (dà wù), thick fog made of tiny water drops.
hint: Use 大雾 to describe a day with very low visibility.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 雾: fog

story:
Rain is the meaning clue in 露; 路 helps with sound.

The rain clue helps with 露水 (lù shuǐ), dew on plants.
hint: 露水 refers to the water droplets found on plants at dawn.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 露: dew

story:
The earliest 目 looked like an eye, later turned upright in writing.

The old eye picture gives a clue to 目光 (mù guāng), a person's gaze.
hint: 目光 describes the direction or intensity of someone's look.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 目: eye

story:
Early writing traced the outline of an ear. Listening begins with that simple shape.

The drawn ear still names the body part in 耳朵 (ěr duo), “ear.”
hint: 耳朵 is the standard term for the human ear.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 耳: ear

story:
An early hand showed five fingers reaching from an arm.

A hand's five fingers help recall 双手 (shuāng shǒu), “both hands.”
hint: 双手 is used when referring to using two hands together.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 手: hand

story:
An early form showed a leg and foot. The shape points to the body part used to kick a ball.

Foot is the body-part meaning behind 足球 (zú qiú), football.
hint: 足球 is the common name for the sport of football.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 足: foot; enough

story:
The older 頭 used 頁, a head-related part, with 豆 as a sound clue.

The head meaning remains in 头发 (tóu fa), the hair on your head.
hint: 头发 specifically refers to the hair on one's head.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 头: head

story:
The earliest 心 was shaped like a heart. The modern character keeps only a few quick strokes of it.

The heart shape leads to 小心 (xiǎo xīn), the everyday warning “be careful.”
hint: 小心 is a common phrase for being cautious or careful.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 心: heart

story:
Early writing drew a person with the middle of the body emphasized. Its meaning widened from the belly to the body.

The old focus on the torso widened to the whole body, as in 身体 (shēn tǐ).
hint: 身体 refers to the physical body of a person.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 身: body

story:
Turn an early form sideways and you can see upper and lower teeth meeting.

The early crossing teeth point to 牙齿 (yá chǐ), the word for teeth.
hint: 牙齿 is the standard word for teeth.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 牙: tooth

story:
An early picture showed a tongue sticking out of a mouth, with little marks near its tip.

The old tongue picture is still the body part named by 舌头 (shé tou).
hint: Use 舌头 to talk about the tongue in your mouth.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 舌: tongue

story:
The old nose picture 自 sits inside the traditional form 鼻; another part helped supply its sound.

The old nose picture helps identify 鼻子 (bí zi), the nose.
hint: 鼻子 is the standard word for your nose.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 鼻: nose

story:
The flesh component 月 gives a body clue, while 僉 supplied the sound in the older 臉.

The flesh clue belongs with 洗脸 (xǐ liǎn), “wash the face.”
hint: 洗脸 is the action of washing your face.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 脸: face

story:
目 means eye; 艮 supplies a sound clue. Together they lead you to the eye itself.

The 目 part, eye, helps you recognize 眼睛 (yǎn jing), the everyday word for eyes.
hint: 眼睛 is the common word for eyes.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 眼: eye

story:
The older 髮 highlighted hair on a head. Simplified 发 hides much of that earlier picture.

The older hair-on-a-head meaning is the one used in 头发 (tóu fa), “hair.”
hint: 头发 is the word for hair on the head.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 发: hair

story:
An early 毛 resembled a tuft of hair or an animal's soft coat.

Hair or fur is the earlier meaning; 毛巾 (máo jīn) is a towel, a separate everyday use to learn.
hint: 毛巾 is a towel used for drying.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 毛: hair; fur

story:
Early writing showed a hand taking an animal skin. The meaning expanded to many outer coverings.

The old animal-skin picture leads to 皮肤 (pí fū), human skin.
hint: 皮肤 is the word for human skin.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 皮: skin

story:
An early shape placed blood inside a vessel. You can still see the little container in 血.

Blood in a vessel is a clue to 血液 (xuè yè), the word for blood.
hint: 血液 is the formal word for blood.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 血: blood

story:
Early forms suggested bones supporting one another to make a frame.

Bones supporting one another lead to 骨头 (gǔ tou), an ordinary bone.
hint: 骨头 is the word for a bone.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 骨: bone

story:
田 is a field, and the old 力 showed a farming tool. Together they were used to write 男, man.

Field and farming tool formed the older sign; 男孩 (nán hái) now means “boy.”
hint: 男孩 is the word for a boy.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 男: male

story:
Early 女 drew a woman kneeling, the way people often sat in that period.

The early woman picture is the meaning used in 女孩 (nǚ hái), “girl.”
hint: Used to describe female people, as seen in the word for girl.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 女: female

story:
Early forms emphasized a baby's large head and small moving arms.

The early baby picture survives in 孩子 (hái zi), the everyday word for child.
hint: Refers to a young person, used in the word for child.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 子: child

story:
子 gives the child meaning; 亥 supplies the sound in 孩.

子 gives the child clue in 小孩 (xiǎo hái), “little child.”
hint: Used specifically in the compound word for a small child.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 孩: child

story:
An early 父 showed a hand holding a stone axe, an image once used for father.

The old axe-bearing figure was used for father; 父亲 (fù qīn) is the word “father.”
hint: Formal term for a male parent, used in the word father.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 父: father

story:
The early form added two marks to 女 to indicate a nursing mother.

The early nursing-mother shape leads to 母亲 (mǔ qīn), “mother.”
hint: Formal term for a female parent, used in the word mother.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 母: mother

story:
父 points to father, while 巴 gives a sound clue in 爸.

爸爸 (bà ba) is the familiar two-syllable word for “dad.”
hint: Informal term for father, used in the word dad.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 爸: dad

story:
女 points to a woman, while 马 supplies the sound in 妈. The two parts work in different ways.

妈妈 (mā ma) is the everyday word for “mum”; 马 helps you remember its sound.
hint: Informal term for mother, used in the word mum.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 妈: mum

story:
An early form emphasized a person's open mouth; it was used for an elder brother who directed younger siblings.

The older role of an elder brother is the sense in 兄弟 (xiōng dì), “brothers.”
hint: Refers to an older male sibling, used in the word brothers.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 兄: elder brother

story:
Early 弟 showed cord wound in order around a weapon handle. The sense of order developed into the younger brother.

The old ordered wrapping helps explain the later family-order sense; 弟弟 (dì di) is “younger brother.”
hint: Refers to a younger male sibling, used in the word brother.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 弟: younger brother

story:
女 gives a female-family clue and 且 supplies the sound; the word's family use changed over time.

女 signals a female family member in 姐姐 (jiě jie), “elder sister.”
hint: Refers to an older female sibling, used in the word sister.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 姐: elder sister

story:
女 gives the female-family clue, while 未 supplies the sound in 妹.

女 signals the family meaning and 未 helps with sound in 妹妹 (mèi mei), “younger sister.”
hint: Use 妹妹 to refer to a younger sister.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 妹: younger sister

story:
Two early hand shapes reached together, a picture of friendly cooperation.

The two hands joined in friendship lead to 朋友 (péng you), “friend.”
hint: Part of the word 朋友 for friend.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 友: friend

story:
Early 朋 showed two strings of shells tied together. Shells could serve as valuables long ago.

The old paired shells gave a way to write 朋; today 朋友 (péng you) means “friend.”
hint: Combine with 友 to mean friend.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 朋: friend

story:
The old 師 first referred to a military group; its meaning later extended to a teacher or master.

From a military group to an expert who guides others, 师 now appears in 老师 (lǎo shī), “teacher.”
hint: Use 老师 to address a teacher.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 师: teacher

story:
A sprout pushing up through the earth was the early picture behind 生, life and growth.

The sprout coming up from earth gives a growth clue in 学生 (xué sheng), “student.”
hint: Use 学生 to describe a student.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 生: life; student

story:
The old 我 pictured a saw. Its use for “I” came from borrowing the sound, not from a picture of a person.

The borrowed pronoun 我 means “I”; adding 们 gives 我们 (wǒ men), “we.”
hint: Use 我 to say I or me.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 我: I; me

story:
你 is a second-person pronoun, “you.”

你好 (nǐ hǎo) is the greeting “hello”; 你 refers to the person being greeted.
hint: Use 你好 to say hello.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 你: you

story:
The person stroke 亻 can remind you that 他 refers to someone else, “he.”

Add 们 to 他 to get 他们 (tā men), “they” for a male or mixed group.
hint: Use 他们 for they or them.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 他: he; him

story:
The person is female in 她; the 女 part distinguishes the written word for “she.”

Add 们 to 她 to get 她们 (tā men), “they” for a female group.
hint: Use 她们 for they or them (female).
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 她: she; her

story:
An early 老 looked like an older person with long hair and a walking stick.

The elderly figure in the old shape still fits 老人 (lǎo rén), “elderly person.”
hint: Use 老人 to refer to an elderly person.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 老: old

story:
An early form brought 女 and 子 together in a close family scene. It was used for affection or goodness.

The early family scene gives a memory link to 好人 (hǎo rén), “good person.”
hint: Use with 'rén' to describe a kind person.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 好: good

story:
The older 愛 contains 心, heart.

The heart in older 愛 connects to 爱心 (ài xīn), a caring heart.
hint: Use with 'xīn' to describe a kind heart.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 爱: love

story:
竹 and 夭 are components of 笑, a character meaning smile or laugh.

大笑 (dà xiào) means “laugh loudly”; the character 笑 can also name a smile.
hint: Use with 'dà' to describe loud laughter.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 笑: laugh; smile

story:
Two 口 parts appear at the top of 哭, which means to cry.

哭声 (kū shēng) is the sound of crying; 哭 can name both crying and the act of crying.
hint: Use with 'shēng' to describe the sound of crying.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 哭: cry

story:
Hand 手 above eye 目 suggests shading your eyes as you look into the distance.

The hand-and-eye construction helps recall 看书 (kàn shū), “read a book.”
hint: Use with 'shū' to describe reading a book.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 看: look; watch

story:
听 means listen; its older traditional form is 聽.

听说 (tīng shuō) means “hear that”; 听 supplies the listening action.
hint: Use with 'shuō' to mean 'I heard that'.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 听: listen

story:
The older 說 carried speech 言 and a sound clue. The simplified 说 keeps a small speech mark on the left.

The speech component helps recall 说话 (shuō huà), “speak.”
hint: Use with 'huà' to describe the act of speaking.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 说: speak

story:
Early 學 pictured hands guiding a child through counting. Learning was already part of its shape.

The early learning scene leads directly to 学习 (xué xí), “study.”
hint: Use with 'xí' to describe the act of studying.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 学: learn

story:
Early 米 represented scattered rice grains.

Rice grains in the old form are the same food named by 大米 (dà mǐ), “rice.”
hint: Use with 'dà' to refer to rice as food.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 米: rice grains

story:
For food, simplified 面 also stands for older 麵, which linked grain with a sound clue.

For this food sense, 面条 (miàn tiáo) names noodles made from flour.
hint: Use with 'tiáo' to describe a bowl of noodles.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 面: noodles; flour

story:
The older 飯 joined a food sign with 反 for sound. It first referred to eating, then to cooked rice or a meal.

The shift from eating to the food eaten explains 米饭 (mǐ fàn), cooked rice.
hint: Use 米饭 to talk about cooked rice as a staple food.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 饭: cooked rice; meal

story:
The plant top supplies the vegetable clue; 采 helped with the sound in 菜.

The plant top helps with 白菜 (bái cài), Chinese cabbage.
hint: Use 白菜 for the specific vegetable known as Chinese cabbage.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 菜: vegetable; dish

story:
Tea once used an older plant-related character. Today's 茶 still wears the plant top.

The plant clue remains useful in 喝茶 (hē chá), “drink tea.”
hint: Use 喝茶 when you want to say drink tea.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 茶: tea

story:
女 is the meaning clue, while 乃 supplies sound. The older sense concerned nursing or the breast.

From nursing to milk, 奶 now appears in 牛奶 (niú nǎi), cow's milk.
hint: Use 牛奶 to refer specifically to cow's milk.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 奶: milk

story:
The older 湯 joined water with 昜 as a sound clue. Its early meaning was hot water.

Its early hot-water sense helps recall 喝汤 (hē tāng), “drink soup.”
hint: Use 喝汤 to describe the action of drinking soup.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 汤: soup

story:
The early 肉 looked like a piece of animal meat. Its folds became lines inside the modern form.

The old meat picture is still the meaning in 牛肉 (niú ròu), beef.
hint: Use 牛肉 to specify beef in your meals.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 肉: meat

story:
Early 魚 was drawn like a fish, with head, body, and tail. Simplified 鱼 keeps a compact outline.

The fish picture leads to 小鱼 (xiǎo yú), a small fish.
hint: Use 小鱼 to describe a small fish.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 鱼: fish

story:
虫 is an animal-related clue in 蛋; another part supplied its sound. The word names an egg.

The animal-related component fits 鸡蛋 (jī dàn), a chicken egg.
hint: Use 鸡蛋 to refer to a chicken egg.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 蛋: egg

story:
An early 瓜 looked like a gourd hanging from a vine.

The old fruit-on-a-vine picture helps recall 西瓜 (xī guā), watermelon.
hint: Use 西瓜 to talk about watermelon.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 瓜: melon

story:
Early 果 drew fruit growing on a tree. The 木 below still gives you a tree to remember.

Fruit on a tree is the meaning carried into 水果 (shuǐ guǒ), the word for fruit.
hint: Use 水果 as a general term for fruit.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 果: fruit

story:
Ancient 豆 first pictured a serving vessel. Its later use for beans is a separate meaning to learn.

The vessel was the older meaning; 豆子 (dòu zi) is the later word for beans.
hint: Use 豆子 to talk about beans in a meal.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 豆: bean

story:
米 gives a grain clue, while 唐 supplies the sound in 糖.

The grain clue fits 糖果 (táng guǒ), sweets made with sugar.
hint: Use 糖果 when referring to candy or sweets.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 糖: sugar; sweet

story:
The older 鹽 carried a salt-related part and a sound clue. The simplified 盐 no longer shows that structure clearly.

The older salt meaning continues in 食盐 (shí yán), table salt.
hint: Use 食盐 for the salt used in cooking.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 盐: salt

story:
The water strokes give a liquid clue, while 由 helps with sound.

The liquid clue helps identify 食用油 (shí yòng yóu), cooking oil.
hint: Use 食用油 for oil used in cooking.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 油: oil

story:
An old form included 酉, associated with fermented liquids. Its sour-taste meaning is familiar today.

The earlier link with fermented liquids fits 酸奶 (suān nǎi), yoghurt with a sour taste.
hint: Use 酸奶 to order or describe yoghurt.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 酸: sour

story:
舌, tongue, meets 甘, sweet, in 甜. The taste is right there on the tongue.

Tongue plus sweet points directly to 甜瓜 (tián guā), a sweet melon.
hint: Use 甜瓜 to describe a sweet melon.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 甜: sweet

story:
The plant top gives a clue to the old bitter herb; 古 supplies the sound.

The bitter-herb meaning helps recall 苦瓜 (kǔ guā), bitter melon.
hint: Use 苦瓜 to refer to bitter melon.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 苦: bitter

story:
辛 points to a sharp taste, while the other part helped with sound.

The sharp-taste clue explains 辣椒 (là jiāo), chilli pepper.
hint: Use 辣椒 to talk about spicy peppers.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 辣: spicy

story:
An early explanation links 香 to the good smell of cooked grain. Let the scent lead you to the kitchen.

The earlier smell of cooked grain broadens to 香味 (xiāng wèi), a pleasant smell.
hint: Use 香味 to describe a good scent.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 香: fragrant

story:
The traditional 飽 uses the food part and 包 as a sound clue. The simplified 饱 keeps that pattern.

The food part and the meaning “eat enough” meet in 吃饱 (chī bǎo), “eat until full.”
hint: Use 吃饱 to express being full after eating.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 饱: full after eating

story:
The food part marks the topic, while 我 supplies the sound in the older 餓. Hunger makes food hard to ignore.

The food part helps recall 饿了 (è le), “hungry now.”
hint: Use this to describe the feeling of needing food.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 饿: hungry

story:
吃 once had a sense related to stumbling over speech. Its everyday meaning now is to eat.

The modern eating meaning is used in 吃饭 (chī fàn), “eat a meal”; the older speech meaning is different.
hint: Use this verb for consuming any type of food.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 吃: eat

story:
Older 喝 could mean “thirsty.” Today the same written character names the action of drinking.

The older sense “thirsty” and today's “drink” meet in 喝水 (hē shuǐ), “drink water.”
hint: Use this verb for consuming liquids like water or tea.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 喝: drink

story:
煮 means to boil or cook.

煮饭 (zhǔ fàn) is “cook rice,” a direct example of 煮 meaning boil or cook.
hint: Use this for preparing food by boiling in water.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 煮: boil; cook

story:
火 is fire; 少 supplies the sound. The pan needs heat and quick movement for stir-frying.

Fire and movement are part of 炒菜 (chǎo cài), “stir-fry dishes.”
hint: Use this for cooking food quickly in a pan.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 炒: stir-fry

story:
The traditional 燒 has fire as its meaning clue and another part for sound.

The fire clue helps with 烧水 (shāo shuǐ), “boil water.”
hint: Use this for heating liquids or cooking with fire.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 烧: burn; cook

story:
Fire 火 gives the heat clue, while 考 supplies the sound in 烤.

The fire clue helps with 烤肉 (kǎo ròu), “roast meat.”
hint: Use this for cooking food using dry oven heat.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 烤: roast; bake

story:
Long ago, 蒸 named the inner stalk of hemp, which could be used as fuel. Cooking with steam is a later meaning.

In 蒸鱼 (zhēng yú), 蒸 names the cooking method: fish cooked by steam.
hint: Use this for cooking food using hot steam.
visual: Three curls of steam rise above a fish.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 蒸: steam

story:
碗 means a bowl, a deep vessel for food or drink.

饭碗 (fàn wǎn) is a rice bowl, one common kind of 碗.
hint: Use this noun for the container used for soup.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 碗: bowl

story:
木 points to a wooden vessel, while 不 helped with sound in 杯.

The older wooden-vessel sense leads to 水杯 (shuǐ bēi), a drinking cup.
hint: Use this noun for a container used for drinking.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 杯: cup

story:
The old form grew from a wash basin. Later 盤 became a word for a plate or tray.

The old basin sense leads to 盘子 (pán zi), an everyday plate.
hint: Use this word when talking about the dishware for serving food.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 盘: plate

story:
The bamboo top hints at the material of early chopsticks, while 快 gives the sound.

The bamboo part recalls the long sticks in 筷子 (kuài zi), chopsticks.
hint: Commonly used in the compound 筷子 for the eating utensil.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 筷: chopstick

story:
An early 勺 looked like a tool for scooping food or liquid.

The old scooping-tool shape is still useful for 勺子 (sháo zi), a spoon.
hint: Used in the compound 勺子 to refer to a spoon.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 勺: spoon

story:
Early 刀 showed a blade and its handle.

The blade-and-handle picture points to 菜刀 (cài dāo), a kitchen knife.
hint: Used in the compound 菜刀 for a kitchen knife.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 刀: knife

story:
The food part belongs to eating; the rest helped with sound. Today 餐 can name a meal.

The older eating sense stays in 早餐 (zǎo cān), breakfast.
hint: Used in the compound 早餐 to mean breakfast.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 餐: meal

story:
The food part gives the topic, while 并 supplies sound in 饼, a baked or steamed flour food.

The food part fits 饼干 (bǐng gān), a baked biscuit.
hint: Used in the compound 饼干 to mean biscuit or cookie.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 饼: flat cake

story:
The oldest form emphasized a chicken's comb and open beak. The modern simplified 鸡 looks quite different.

The early chicken picture still names the bird in 鸡肉 (jī ròu), chicken meat.
hint: Used in the compound 鸡肉 to refer to chicken meat.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 鸡: chicken

story:
The older 鴨 combined a bird sign with 甲 for sound. Simplified 鸭 keeps the bird on the right.

The bird clue gives the animal in 鸭子 (yā zi), duck.
hint: Used in the compound 鸭子 to refer to a duck.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 鸭: duck

story:
Early 牛 showed a cow's head from the front, with two curved horns.

The horned head in the early form names the animal in 牛肉 (niú ròu), beef.
hint: Used in the compound 牛肉 to refer to beef.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 牛: cow

story:
Early 羊 showed a sheep's head and its curled horns.

The curved horns in the early form name the animal in 羊肉 (yáng ròu), mutton.
hint: Used in the compound 羊肉 to refer to mutton.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 羊: sheep

story:
The older 豬 joined a pig sign with 者 for sound. Simplified 猪 hides the old animal sign.

The older pig sign gives the animal in 猪肉 (zhū ròu), pork.
hint: Use 猪肉 to talk about pork in a restaurant or market.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 猪: pig

story:
An older meaning of 蝦 referred to a frog or toad. Today the character commonly names shrimp.

The older frog-related sense shifted; 大虾 (dà xiā) now names a large shrimp.
hint: Use 大虾 to describe a large-sized shrimp.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 虾: shrimp

story:
虫 marks an animal-related meaning, while 解 helps supply the sound in 蟹.

The animal-related part fits 螃蟹 (páng xiè), crab.
hint: Use 螃蟹 to refer to a crab.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 蟹: crab

story:
木 marks a tree, while 兆 supplies a sound clue. The fruit grows on that tree.

The tree component points to the fruit in 桃子 (táo zi), peach.
hint: Use 桃子 when buying or eating a peach.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 桃: peach

story:
木 points to the pear tree, while the upper part helped with sound.

The tree component points to the fruit in 梨子 (lí zi), pear.
hint: Use 梨子 to refer to a pear.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 梨: pear

story:
The older 蘋 named a water plant; later it became part of the word for apple. Learn 苹果 as a whole word.

The older water-plant sense differs from 苹果 (píng guǒ), the everyday word for apple.
hint: Use 苹果 to talk about an apple.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 苹: apple (in 苹果)

story:
木 gives a tree clue, while 登 supplies the sound in 橙, an orange.

The tree clue points to the fruit in 橙子 (chéng zi), orange.
hint: Use 橙子 to refer to an orange.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 橙: orange

story:
The food part leads to a meal, while 交 helps with sound in 饺, a filled dumpling.

The food part fits 饺子 (jiǎo zi), a filled dumpling.
hint: Use 饺子 to order or describe a dumpling.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 饺: dumpling (in 饺子)

story:
Early 家 placed a pig beneath a roof, suggesting livestock kept at home.

The old roof-and-pig scene named a household; 回家 (huí jiā) means “go home.”
hint: Use 回家 to say you are going home.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 家: home; family

story:
Early 門 looked like two doors side by side. Simplified 门 preserves a doorway outline.

The early pair of doors explains 开门 (kāi mén), “open the door.”
hint: Use 开门 to ask someone to open the door.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 门: door

story:
窗 means window, an opening that lets light and air into a room.

窗户 (chuāng hu) is the everyday word for a window.
hint: Use 窗户 for window in daily conversation.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 窗: window

story:
戶 supplied a door or room clue, while 方 supplied sound in the older 房.

The old door clue belongs to 房间 (fáng jiān), “room.”
hint: 房间 refers to a specific room.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 房: room; house

story:
The old 屋 combined parts associated with a dwelling and a place to settle.

The dwelling meaning stays in 屋子 (wū zi), “house.”
hint: 屋子 is a common word for house.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 屋: house

story:
A roof sits above 至, a part associated with arriving or stopping. Together they pointed to a room where people stay.

The roof-and-rest idea belongs in 教室 (jiào shì), a classroom.
hint: 教室 is the standard word for classroom.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 室: room

story:
厅 means a hall or a larger room used for gathering.

客厅 (kè tīng) is the living room, a kind of hall in a home.
hint: 客厅 is the living room area.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 厅: hall

story:
床 means a bed, the piece of furniture used for sleeping.

上床 (shàng chuáng) means “go to bed,” using 床 for bed.
hint: 上床 means to go to bed.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 床: bed

story:
木 points to a wooden object, while 卓 supplies the sound in 桌, a table.

The wood clue fits 桌子 (zhuō zi), table.
hint: 桌子 is the word for table.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 桌: table

story:
木 points to wood, while 奇 supplies sound. 椅 originally also named a tree before it became a chair.

The wood clue fits 椅子 (yǐ zi), chair.
hint: 椅子 is the word for chair.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 椅: chair

story:
Fire is the meaning clue in 灯, while 登 supplies the sound. A lamp brings light into a dark room.

The fire-and-light clue helps with 电灯 (diàn dēng), electric light.
hint: 电灯 refers to an electric light.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 灯: lamp

story:
The old 書 included a hand holding a writing brush. It first named the act of writing.

From writing to written pages, 书 now appears in 书本 (shū běn), a book.
hint: 书本 is the word for books.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 书: book

story:
The old writing tool 聿 gained a bamboo top to make 筆. Simplified 笔 still shows bamboo above.

The old brush construction fits 毛笔 (máo bǐ), a writing brush.
hint: Used for writing; 毛笔 is a traditional brush.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 笔: pen

story:
The older 紙 used a thread-related part with 氏 for sound. The simplified 纸 keeps that pattern.

The thread-related older form now names 白纸 (bái zhǐ), white paper.
hint: Material for writing; 白纸 is white paper.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 纸: paper

story:
An early 包 suggested a baby enclosed in the womb. Its meaning spread to wrapping and bags.

From enclosing something to carrying it, 包 appears in 书包 (shū bāo), schoolbag.
hint: Container for items; 书包 is a schoolbag.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 包: bag

story:
Early 衣 looked like a garment.

The old garment picture leads to 衣服 (yī fu), clothes.
hint: Garments worn; 衣服 means clothes.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 衣: clothing

story:
The leather part 革 marks footwear, while 圭 supplies sound in 鞋.

The leather clue fits 鞋子 (xié zi), shoes.
hint: Footwear; 鞋子 means shoes.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 鞋: shoe

story:
Early 車 showed the parts of a cart: wheels, body, and axle. Simplified 车 keeps only a few strokes.

The old cart picture expanded to vehicles such as 汽车 (qì chē), car.
hint: Mode of transport; 汽车 means a car.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 车: vehicle

story:
Early 馬 was a horse with body and mane. Simplified 马 makes the animal much harder to see.

The old horse picture is the animal pulling 马车 (mǎ chē), a horse-drawn cart.
hint: Animal used for riding; 马车 is a carriage.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 马: horse

story:
足 gives a walking clue, while 各 supplies sound. 路 is the path your feet follow.

The foot clue fits 马路 (mǎ lù), road, a place for travel.
hint: Path for travel; 马路 is a road.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 路: road

story:
The older 街 used 行, a road-related part, with 圭 for sound.

The road part fits 大街 (dà jiē), main street.
hint: Public thoroughfare; 大街 is a main street.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 街: street

story:
木 points to a wooden structure, while 喬 supplied sound in the older 橋.

The wood clue fits 大桥 (dà qiáo), large bridge.
hint: Structure over water; 大桥 is a large bridge.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 桥: bridge

story:
广 suggests a roofed place, while 占 supplies sound in 店, originally a place for goods.

The older place for goods remains in 书店 (shū diàn), bookshop.
hint: Used for places where you buy goods or stay.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 店: shop

story:
One explanation of early 市 links its shape to the noise of a market. The modern word also appears in “city.”

From market to built-up place, 市 appears in 城市 (chéng shì), city.
hint: Refers to a city or a market area.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 市: city; market

story:
The older 國 marked an enclosed territory, with another part helping its sound. Simplified 国 keeps the border.

The old enclosed territory leads to 中国 (Zhōng guó), China.
hint: Used to describe a nation or country.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 国: country

story:
An early 城 pictured a defended settlement and its walls. The modern form names a city.

The defended settlement became the city named in 城市 (chéng shì).
hint: Refers to a city or a walled area.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 城: city

story:
木 gives a rural tree clue, while 寸 supplies sound in 村, a village.

The rural settlement sense is still in 村子 (cūn zi), village.
hint: Used for a small rural settlement.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 村: village

story:
木 and 交 formed 校, which first named a wooden restraint. Its familiar modern use is in “school.”

The older wooden-tool meaning changed; 学校 (xué xiào) now means school.
hint: Used in words related to education.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 校: school (in 学校)

story:
The old 院 meant an enclosing wall. The modern word appears in names of many institutions.

From an enclosing wall to an institution, 院 appears in 医院 (yī yuàn), hospital.
hint: Used for institutions or courtyards.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 院: courtyard; institution

story:
立 points to standing, while 占 supplies sound. A station is where travelers stand and wait.

Standing and waiting connects to 车站 (chē zhàn), station.
hint: Used for transit stops or standing.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 站: station; stand

story:
The older 機 first named a trigger mechanism. The meaning expanded to machines of many kinds.

From a trigger mechanism to machines, 机 appears in 飞机 (fēi jī), airplane.
hint: Used for machines or mechanical devices.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 机: machine

story:
The older 場 had 土 for ground and 昜 for sound. It first named a flat place for a ceremony.

The earlier flat place leads to 机场 (jī chǎng), airport, a place for aircraft.
hint: Used for open areas or venues.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 场: open area; venue

story:
舟 points to a boat, while the other part supplies sound.

The boat component fits 小船 (xiǎo chuán), a small boat.
hint: Use this for water transport like a small boat.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 船: boat

story:
The water part marks a waterway; the older sense was a small channel linked to a river or lake.

The old waterway sense leads to 港口 (gǎng kǒu), harbour.
hint: Refers to a harbour or port area.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 港: harbour

story:
The older 島 used 山 for land and 鳥 as a sound clue.

The land-and-sea meaning fits 小岛 (xiǎo dǎo), a small island.
hint: Used for land surrounded by water.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 岛: island

story:
The old 園 had an enclosing border, fitting a garden surrounded by a fence.

The old enclosed garden sense remains in 公园 (gōng yuán), park.
hint: Refers to a garden or public park.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 园: garden; park

story:
An early interpretation sees 公 as a vessel; the word later came to mean public or shared.

The later “shared” meaning is used in 公共 (gōng gòng), public.
hint: Means public or shared by everyone.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 公: public

story:
Early 工 may have pictured a tool with a working edge. It later came to name skill and work.

One interpretation of the old tool shape connects with 工作 (gōng zuò), work.
hint: Refers to work or a job.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 工: work

story:
厂 means factory in the everyday word 工厂.

工厂 (gōng chǎng) names a factory, a place where things are made.
hint: Refers to a factory or industrial building.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 厂: factory

story:
木 is the meaning clue in the older 樓; 婁 supplies sound. Today 楼 can name a building or one floor.

The older multi-storey building meaning fits 高楼 (gāo lóu), tall building.
hint: Refers to a building or a floor.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 楼: building; floor

story:
木 points to a wooden object, while 弟 supplies sound. A 梯 helps you climb.

The wooden climbing tool gave the meaning used in 楼梯 (lóu tī), stairs.
hint: Refers to stairs or a ladder.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 梯: stairs; ladder

story:
Early 牆 related to the enclosing walls of a grain store. The simplified 墙 still names a wall.

The old enclosing-wall sense fits 墙上 (qiáng shàng), “on the wall.”
hint: Refers to a wall in a room.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 墙: wall

story:
Early 走 showed a person swinging both arms while running. Its everyday meaning later shifted to walking.

The older running picture changed to the everyday walking sense in 走路 (zǒu lù).
hint: Use 走路 to talk about the action of walking.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 走: walk

story:
足 points to a foot, while 包 supplies sound.

The foot clue matches 跑步 (pǎo bù), “run.”
hint: Use 跑步 to describe the sport or action of running.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 跑: run

story:
来 means come.

回来 (huí lái) means “come back,” with 来 supplying the coming direction.
hint: Use 回来 to express the action of returning or coming back.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 来: come

story:
An old explanation links 去 with an open mouth; its familiar later use is “go away.”

From leaving to 出去 (chū qù), “go out,” 去 marks movement away.
hint: Use 出去 to describe the action of going outside.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 去: go

story:
Early 回 traced a turning or circling path. Returning follows that path back.

The old circling path leads to 回家 (huí jiā), “go home.”
hint: Use 回家 to talk about returning to your home.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 回: return

story:
An early 開 showed hands removing a bar from a door. The door could open at last.

The old unbarred gate explains 开门 (kāi mén), “open the door.”
hint: Use 开门 to describe the action of opening a door.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 开: open

story:
An old 關 pictured a gate held shut with bars. Simplified 关 no longer shows the gate.

The old barred gate explains 关门 (guān mén), “close the door.”
hint: Use 关门 to describe the action of closing a door.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 关: close

story:
An old form showed someone kneeling on the ground, the usual way to sit in ancient times.

The old kneeling posture is the action in 坐下 (zuò xià), “sit down.”
hint: Use 坐下 to describe the action of sitting down.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 坐: sit

story:
One horizontal stroke has represented the number one since the earliest writing.

That single line is the number used in 一个 (yí ge), “one item.”
hint: Use 一个 as a common way to count one object.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 一: one

story:
Two horizontal strokes count two. Early 二 already looked much like the character you write now.

The two lines give the number in 二月 (èr yuè), February, the second month.
hint: Use 二月 to refer to the second month, February.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 二: two

story:
Three lines count three. Early writing used the same simple idea.

The three lines give the number in 三天 (sān tiān), “three days.”
hint: Use 三 to count items or time periods like three days.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 三: three

story:
An early form used four horizontal marks, one for each item counted. The modern shape changed later.

Four old marks gave the number in 四季 (sì jì), the four seasons.
hint: Use 四 to describe groups of four, such as four seasons.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 四: four

story:
The original meaning of the shape of 五 is disputed. Its established use is the number five.

五个 (wǔ ge) means five items; no picture of five objects is needed to learn 五.
hint: Use 五 followed by a measure word for five objects.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 五: five

story:
Some early forms of 六 resembled 入. Its use for the number six developed long ago.

The old sign became the number used in 六月 (liù yuè), June, the sixth month.
hint: Use 六 before 月 to name the month of June.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 六: six

story:
One explanation sees 七 as a line cutting across another; its use for seven came later.

The borrowed number meaning is the one in 七天 (qī tiān), “seven days.”
hint: Use 七 to count seven days or seven items.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 七: seven

story:
The two strokes of 八 lean away from one another, an early idea of separating; the number use came later.

The number use is the one in 八月 (bā yuè), August, the eighth month.
hint: Use 八 before 月 to name the month of August.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 八: eight

story:
An early 九 resembled a bent arm or elbow. The same shape was borrowed to write nine.

The elbow shape was borrowed for the number in 九个 (jiǔ ge), “nine items.”
hint: Use 九 followed by a measure word for nine objects.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 九: nine

story:
Early 十 was often just one vertical mark. Later writing changed it to the cross you see now.

The old vertical mark became the number in 十天 (shí tiān), “ten days.”
hint: Use 十 to count ten days or ten items.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 十: ten

story:
Early 百 combined 一 with 白 to write one hundred.

The old “one hundred” combination is still read in 一百 (yì bǎi).
hint: Use 百 to express quantities in the hundreds.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 百: hundred

story:
An early 千 added a mark to 人 to write one thousand. It became a number far beyond counting on fingers.

The old “one thousand” combination is still read in 一千 (yì qiān).
hint: Use 千 to express quantities in the thousands.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 千: thousand

story:
An early form of 萬 resembled a scorpion; its number meaning came from borrowing the character.

The borrowed number meaning is the one in 一万 (yí wàn), “ten thousand.”
hint: Used for large numbers like ten thousand.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 万: ten thousand

story:
The older 零 joined rain with 令 for sound. Its modern use as zero came later.

The older falling-rain sense changed; in 零个 (líng ge), 零 means zero.
hint: Used to represent zero or nothing.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 零: zero

story:
An early 兩 showed a pair of yokes on a cart. That paired image suits the number two.

The old paired-yoke picture fits 两个 (liǎng ge), “two items.”
hint: Used for the quantity of two.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 两: two (before a measure word)

story:
An early 半 was understood as dividing an ox into two parts. From dividing came the idea of half.

The old division into two leads to 半天 (bàn tiān), “half a day.”
hint: Used to describe half of something.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 半: half

story:
The older 雙 showed two birds together with a hand. The pair gives a clue to “double.”

The old pair of birds points to 双手 (shuāng shǒu), “both hands.”
hint: Used for pairs or both of something.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 双: pair; double

story:
An early 單 may have pictured a simple weapon. Its present sense of “single” came later.

One proposed old weapon sense differs from today's 单人 (dān rén), “single-person.”
hint: Used for single or individual items.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 单: single

story:
Early 多 used two pieces of meat; in one interpretation, two pieces already seemed plentiful.

Two pieces in the old form gave the idea of many; 多少 (duō shao) asks “how many?”
hint: Used to ask about quantity.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 多: many; much

story:
Early 少 grew from tiny marks, like 小, “small.” It came to mean few or little.

Small marks gave a word for few or little; 少量 (shǎo liàng) means “small amount.”
hint: Used for small quantities.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 少: few; little

story:
The oldest meaning of 今 is disputed.

今天 (jīn tiān) means today, the current day; the old shape's first meaning remains uncertain.
hint: Used to refer to the present day.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 今: now; current

story:
日 and 月 are visible in 明. The character can mean bright and also appears in time words.

明天 (míng tiān) means tomorrow, while 明 can also mean bright.
hint: Used to refer to the next day.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 明: bright; next

story:
日 gives the day clue, while 乍 supplies sound. 昨 points to the day just before today.

The sun clue marks a day, and 昨天 (zuó tiān) is the day before today.
hint: Use 昨天 to talk about the day before today.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 昨: previous (day)

story:
Early 年 showed a person carrying harvested grain. A harvest marked the turning of a year.

The old harvest picture helps recall 今年 (jīn nián), “this year.”
hint: Use 今年 to refer to the current calendar year.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 年: year

story:
The older 歲 used a walking-related form, fitting the passing of years. Simplified 岁 is much shorter.

The passing-years sense is used in 三岁 (sān suì), “three years old.”
hint: Use 岁 to describe a person's age in years.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 岁: year of age

story:
The older 時 included the sun 日, a clue to days and time, with another part for sound.

The sun-and-time clue helps with 小时 (xiǎo shí), “hour.”
hint: Use 小时 to measure a duration of sixty minutes.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 时: time; hour

story:
Early 分 paired a knife with two parts moving apart. It first meant divide or separate.

From dividing into parts to dividing time, 分 appears in 分钟 (fēn zhōng), “minute.”
hint: Use 分钟 to talk about a specific minute duration.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 分: minute; divide

story:
禾 gives a grain clue, while 少 supplies sound. 秒 once named the fine point of a grain stalk.

From a tiny grain point to a tiny unit of time, 秒 appears in 一秒 (yì miǎo), “one second.”
hint: Use 秒 for the smallest unit of time here.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 秒: second (time)

story:
The older 點 combined black with a sound clue. Its first sense was a small dark mark.

The small-mark sense broadened; 三点 (sān diǎn) tells the time, “three o’clock.”
hint: Use 点 to tell the time on a clock.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 点: dot; o’clock

story:
An early 早 joined the rising sun with a sign of beginning: the start of the day.

The rising-sun clue is the time of day in 早上 (zǎo shang), “morning.”
hint: Use 早上 to refer to the early morning period.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 早: early; morning

story:
日 gives a day clue, while 免 supplies sound. The sun is near its end in the evening.

The day ending is the time in 晚上 (wǎn shang), “evening.”
hint: Use 晚上 to talk about the evening or night.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 晚: late; evening

story:
An early 午 looked like a wooden pestle for pounding grain. Its use in noon is a later development.

The old pestle shape was borrowed for the noon sense in 中午 (zhōng wǔ).
hint: Use 中午 to refer to the middle of the day.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 午: noon

story:
夜 has long named the time opposite daytime.

The old night meaning remains in 夜晚 (yè wǎn), “night.”
hint: Use this word to describe the time after sunset.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 夜: night

story:
Early 周 may have pictured a carved object. The familiar meaning “week” came much later.

One proposed early meaning concerns carving; 周末 (zhōu mò) now means “weekend.”
hint: Refers to a seven-day cycle or a weekend.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 周: week; cycle

story:
An old form used sun or moon as a time clue, with 其 supplying sound. 期 names a period.

The time clue continues in 星期 (xīng qī), the word for week.
hint: Used to denote a specific duration or week.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 期: period of time

story:
Early 季 combined a young child with a grain plant. Its uses later expanded, including “season.”

The old sense of youth changed; 四季 (sì jì) means the four seasons.
hint: Used to talk about the four seasons.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 季: season

story:
An early 每 showed a woman with a hairpin. Its everyday sense “every” came through later usage.

The earlier hairpin picture changed in use; 每天 (měi tiān) now means “every day.”
hint: Use this to indicate every instance or day.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 每: every

story:
An old 次 may have pictured someone speaking; its use for counting occasions came later.

One proposed early speaking sense differs from 一次 (yí cì), “one time.”
hint: Use this to count how many times something happens.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 次: time; occurrence

story:
个 is a common measure word.

This measure word counts items in 三个 (sān ge), “three items.”
hint: A common word to count general objects.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 个: general measure word

story:
木 is a tree, and an early mark at its base pointed to the root. 本 later became a book measure word.

The old mark at a tree's root became a measure word in 一本书 (yì běn shū), “one book.”
hint: Use this to count books or bound documents.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 本: book measure word; root

story:
The older 張 included a bow and a sound clue; an early meaning involved drawing the bowstring tight.

The old stretched-bow sense broadened; 一张纸 (yì zhāng zhǐ) counts “one sheet of paper.”
hint: Use this to count flat objects like paper.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 张: measure word for flat things

story:
土 gives an earth clue; older 塊 first meant a lump of earth. Today 块 also counts pieces or yuan.

The earth-clod meaning broadened; 一块钱 (yí kuài qián) is one yuan in everyday prices.
hint: Used for currency or chunks of items.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 块: piece; yuan (colloquial)

story:
One old form showed a hand catching a bird. Today 只 can count some animals, as in one cat.

The old caught-bird picture changed in use; 一只猫 (yì zhī māo) counts “one cat.”
hint: Use this word to count individual animals.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 只: measure word for some animals

story:
第 grew from an older order-related word. Its bamboo top helps distinguish it in the modern character.

The old order sense survives in 第一 (dì yī), “first.”
hint: Add this before numbers to show order.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 第: ordinal prefix

story:
Early 先 placed a foot ahead of a person: someone going first.

The foot ahead of a person gives the order in 先来 (xiān lái), “come first.”
hint: Use this to describe what happens before others.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 先: first; before

story:
The original shape of 再 is uncertain; its modern meaning is “again.”

再见 (zài jiàn) means goodbye; 再 carries the idea of seeing someone again.
hint: Use this to indicate doing something once more.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 再: again; then

story:
Early 長 showed an elder with long hair and a walking stick. Its uses later included “long.”

The old elder-with-long-hair picture helps recall 长短 (cháng duǎn), “length.”
hint: Use this to describe something that is not short.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 长: long

story:
矢 and 豆 formed 短; the second part helped with sound. The word describes a short distance between ends.

Short distance between two ends is the sense behind 短发 (duǎn fà), “short hair.”
hint: Use this to describe something that is not long.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 短: short

story:
心 marks a feeling, while 夬 supplies sound. 快 first meant happy and later also fast.

From happy to fast, 快 in 快走 (kuài zǒu) means “walk quickly.”
hint: Use this to describe high speed.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 快: fast

story:
心 marks a feeling, while 曼 supplies sound. 慢 once suggested laziness and now commonly means slow.

From a slower, less active sense, 慢 in 慢走 (màn zǒu) means “walk slowly.”
hint: Use this to describe low speed.
imageAlt: Ink-wash learning illustration for 慢: slow
